## Phase 171 / A guard whose own comment said "share one guard", in the file where two readers repeated it

- **Milestone / version:** refactor + one test case + shipped-comment corrections after `0.21.21`. Branch `refactor/trace-metrics-single-guard` off `ad94d3f`.
- **What the sweep was looking for.** Phase 170 closed with "the remaining question there is absolutes rather than counts", so the pass read every comment in `trace.ts`, `port-reaper.ts`, `version.ts`, `worker-mode.ts`, `hooks.ts` and `vue.ts` that claims something is the only one, always, never, or exactly N — and asked of each whether the code still says so.
- **The find: a redundancy that was absorbing a mutant, not saving it.** `metricsActive`'s doc says the getter exists "so the seven readers … share one guard instead of repeating it", and two of those seven — `getMetrics` and `flush` — then appended `|| this.stopped` to the guard whose first operand had just evaluated a term containing `!this.stopped`. Such a read cannot be the decider (one synchronous expression, no intervening code, so the field's value cannot change between the two reads), which is exactly why it looked harmless. Measured instead: deleting the getter's `!stopped` term against that tree left **all 37 test files green**, so the sentence calling the term "part of the contract, not a bonus" had no evidence behind it at all — and the reason none existed is that `flush()`'s own repeat caught the mutation in the one test that walks the sequence. With both repeats deleted, the same deletion fails two tests: the pre-existing `starts a fresh metrics window after pause and resume, and stop prevents later flushes`, and the third case now added to `getMetrics returns null while metrics recording is inactive`, whose name promises all three inactive causes and which tested two of them.
- **What the term actually protects**, now written at the site: `stop()` resets the counters through `pause()` *before* any later call can reach them, so without the term a `record*` during a stopped window accumulates unreset and `start()` — which clears `stopped` and does not reset — hands it to the new session's window. `grep -c "this.metricsActive" src/core/trace.ts` → 7, and `stopped` is read in exactly two places afterwards (the getter's term, and `event()`, which skips metrics and gates on the field itself); both counts re-grepped rather than inherited.
- **An uncovered line that is a typing requirement.** `percentileMs`'s closing `return` — the histogram ceiling, documented as reached "when the rank exceeds all counts" — has never executed and no test can reach it: all six calls pass one of `0.5`/`0.95`/`1` together with this reporter's own `latencySamples`, and `recordDispatched` increments that counter and exactly one bucket in the same synchronous block with nothing between the two that can skip either, so `samples === sum(buckets)` at every read and the rank is inside it. `sampleCount <= 0` returns one line above. Deleting the statement is `TS2366` ("Function lacks ending return statement"), measured on this tree. The prose said a behavior where there is an exhaustiveness requirement, and it names the `0.21.19` non-finite guard as the thing that used to make the leg reachable — which is why the line reads 0 and is not a gap.
- **`version.ts`'s paragraph contradicted its own next clause.** It claimed "Source-level consumers (typecheck, vitest) get the same value via the vitest `define`" while also saying the `declare` "keeps tsc happy when no define is present": `pnpm typecheck` is `tsc --noEmit` and evaluates no code, so it cannot get a value from anywhere. The follow-on sentence's "the only consumer this module is read by at source level" counted two readers as one. Both corrected against `vitest.config.ts` and `scripts/build.mjs`, whose `define` sites all read `version` from `package.json`, and the absolute "can never drift from the release" was rewritten as the actual two-link chain: this constant cannot drift from `package.json`, and `scripts/verify-release-version.mjs` refuses a tag that is not `v` plus that field. No `docs/` file restates the retracted sentence (grepped for `drift`).
- **The method finding, which cost a false `NOT byte-identical`.** The cheap proof that a prose sweep moved no code — esbuild each revision and `cmp` — reported a difference for a change that moved none, because esbuild preserves a comment **only in expression position**: inside a parenthesized initializer, or before a returned expression. A declaration header and a statement slot are both dropped (three-case probe file: `export const x = (// kept…)` emitted, `/** HEADER */` and a comment before `const y = 3` vanished). So `cmp` on the raw output fails on some comment-only edits and passes on others, and neither verdict meant anything until the outputs were compared with comment lines stripped — after which `version.ts` is code-identical at 6 emitted lines. That also narrows the older "the shipped comment surface is the declarations *and* the JS" line: the JS half is the expression-slot subset, not every comment. Rule and correction are in `AGENTS.md`.
- **What came out correct, so nobody re-derives it.** `port-reaper.ts` is the densest comment file in `src/` and every checkable claim in it held: `register()` really does always call `schedule()`; the four `schedule()` call sites are the four the `schedule()` note enumerates, with `setTimeout()` and `remove()` behind `targets.has(port)` and the reap pass behind `reapedAny`; "the two statements that null `handle`" is `grep -c "this.handle = null"` → 2; `targets` gains a port in `register()` only (its three-map write) and loses one in `remove()`, in the reap loop and in `dispose()`'s `clear()` only; `computeMinHeartbeat` starts from `DEFAULT_HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL_MS` (`10_000`, so "never stretch it past 10 s") and only takes a `Math.min`, which is what makes the `0.0001 → 0.0003 ms` arithmetic right (`DEFAULT_SESSION_TIMEOUT_MULTIPLIER` is `3`); "nothing in `tests/` calls `computeMinHeartbeat`" is `grep -rn … tests/` → 0 hits; `dispose()` has no caller in `src/` at all; and `vue.ts`'s `intervalMs: 0` really does leave `timer` null while a reactive interval change re-arms the timer without touching the bus. The vocabulary census behind the sweep, same pattern in each file (`only|never|always|every|exactly|cannot|sole|no-op`, count of matching lines): `port-reaper.ts` and `trace.ts` 28 each, `hooks.ts` 6, `vue.ts` 1, `worker-mode.ts` **0** — so the two large files were read line by line, `hooks.ts`'s three effect-level claims were read against their effect bodies (`useCrossTabDataBus`'s "nothing between the lines below yields" is true because that body has no `await`, so no newer mount can interleave), and `worker-mode.ts` had nothing to check.
- **The same sweep measured the harness's other delivery question, and the verdict is "leave it alone".** Making `ChannelHub` deliver asynchronously — which is what a `BroadcastChannel` actually does — was probed by flipping the field's initializer: **18** cases fail (9 `cluster`, 6 `data-bus`, 1 `stability`, plus 2 in `coordination-invariants` itself), and not one of the assertion messages reads as a wrong end state; every one inspected is a frame that had not arrived when the assertion ran (`expected [] to deeply equal [ 1 ]`, a delivery count off by one). So the flip buys fidelity and has no demonstrated defect kill to show for it — the same question the marginal-kill-rate rule asks of a candidate harness. Those two `coordination-invariants` failures are also why this is a *decision* rather than an oversight: `delivers on a later microtask once a hub opts into browser ordering` asserts `the default hub must keep delivering in the posting stack`, so synchronous delivery is pinned by name. Its comment carried the count as **17 (15 + 2)**; it now carries **18 (16 + 2)** with the per-file split and an instruction to re-measure rather than trust it, because the number moved with the suite — the same drift class as a line-number citation, one step removed since nothing here even breaks.
- **Ledger.** `src/` still holds **47** zero branch arms, now of **1958** instead of 1962 — the four slots that left were the two deleted operands and their hot partners, so the numerator never moved and aggregate branches read **97.60 → 97.59**. That 0.01 is the arithmetic of a smaller denominator, and `trace.ts`'s three arms are the same three it had (the sink arrow default, and the two `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`-required `?? 0`). 923 tests, unchanged: the phase added a case, not a test.
- **Verification:** `pnpm check` 0 (typecheck, build, 923 tests, 5/5 perf gates), `pnpm test:coverage` 0 at `99.02 / 97.59 / 99.27 / 99.69`, `pnpm lint` 0, `pnpm typecheck` 0 after the comment commits. Both mutant runs were printed as a diff before their result was read, and each file was restored from a `/tmp` copy taken before the mutation rather than by hand.
- **Risk / rollback:** two guard operands deleted where the same expression already reads the field synchronously (no input can distinguish them, and the two tests above are the evidence), one test case, five comment blocks and one `AGENTS.md` rule. `git revert` of the branch's two commits restores the file; nothing in the public surface, the frames, the storage keys or the defaults moves, so the three public-surface gates have nothing to report beyond comment text.
- **Next:** the same single-sourcing question one module over — `websocket.ts` guards its asynchronous callbacks with three-field staleness chains (`this.socket !== socket || this.handlers !== handlers || …`) whose fields are *also* read by each other's guards, so the question there is which operand is dominated by another in the same expression rather than by a getter one call away. `replay-persistence.ts`'s six arms stay classified. `pnpm bench:browser` is still deferred on host load.
- **Update date:** 2026-09-24.


## Phase 172 / Which operand of a guard is allowed to decide, in a transport with three-term staleness chains

- **Milestone / version:** test + shipped-comment work after `0.21.21`. Branch `test/websocket-dead-attempt-events` off `7c1b6b5`.
- **The question, inherited from Phase 171.** That phase deleted two `|| this.stopped` operands that a guard one term earlier had already settled, and found the deletion was what made the guard's contract testable. `websocket.ts` is the other place in `src/` where a guard asks the same question three times over, so each operand of each chain was measured on its own rather than reasoned about.
- **The state that makes the last operand the only decider.** `stop()` clears `this.socket`, so operand 1 sees every teardown. But a connect timeout, a `close` and an `error` each lower `socketActive` while leaving `this.socket` naming the *same* object, so for anything that socket delivers afterwards only the third operand can distinguish it — operands 1 and 2 are comparing a pair that still matches.
- **Measured, operand by operand (one deletion at a time, whole suite, 926 tests):** `onclose`'s was already held by three lifecycle cases (`maps socket lifecycle to the DataBus status vocabulary`, `opens a replacement socket after the current connection fails or closes`, `automatically reopens and re-subscribes after a socket error`). `onerror`'s, `onmessage`'s and the one `handleMessage` re-reads after `await raw.arrayBuffer()` each **killed nothing** — three live operands whose behavior no test named. Three cases were added, and each now dies to exactly its own mutant.
- **What the consequence is, per leg:** a second `onStatus('error')` + `onError` for a connection the application was already told had failed; a publication delivered into the handlers of an attempt that timed out; a Blob whose conversion completed after its connection closed arriving as live data.
- **A test that passed green against the mutation it was written for.** The first version of the Blob case delivered a Blob frame to a *timed-out* attempt and asserted non-delivery. It survived the operand deletion for a reason the code states directly: a timed-out socket cannot reach `handleMessage` at all, because `onmessage`'s own guard rejects the frame one step earlier. The premise was unreachable, so the assertion could not fail — and it would have been committed as "this leg is pinned" had the matrix not been re-run *after* the edit rather than before. Rebuilt as: park `arrayBuffer()` on a controllable deferred, fire the frame while the attempt is live, close the connection while the conversion is outstanding, then resolve it. The positive control (same deferred, same frame, connection still open → `onMessage` called with the expected bytes) sits inside the same test, because an undeliverable frame and a correctly dropped one are indistinguishable from `not.toHaveBeenCalled()`.
- **The generalization that would have hidden it:** "the timeout state exercises the dead-socket legs". True for two of the three and false for the Blob path, blocked one guard earlier. Reachability is per-leg, so the state that *enters* a guard has to be checked from the guard's own call site, not from the transport's failure taxonomy.
- **Method note, since it bit the driver.** The site comment added by this phase shifted every line below it, and a mutation script that located guards by line number asserted at the wrong line and named it. The driver now finds the guards by matching the whole stripped condition and resolves each to its owner by scanning back for the enclosing `socket.on* =` or method, printing that map before mutating. Three textually identical `!==` guards and two identical `===` ones exist in the file, so "first match" is not a selector; the occurrence index is, and it is checked against the owner.
- **The one restatement this found by grepping the claim rather than the file.** `AGENTS.md` carried "making *every* hub asynchronous breaks ~16 tests in `cluster`/`data-bus`/`stability`" while the measurement behind it (Phase 171) is 18, of which 2 are the hub's own delivery pins and 16 are post-and-assert cases. `tests/coordination-invariants.test.ts` had already been corrected in the previous PR; this is the second copy of the same sentence, which is the pattern the paraphrase rule exists for.
- **Ledger:** `src/` unchanged at **47** zero branch arms of **1958**, aggregate **99.02 / 97.59 / 99.27 / 99.69**, `websocket.ts` still holding its two classified arms (the `connectPromise ?? undefined` reuse leg and the connect-timer guard). None of the three operands this phase pinned was a zero count — every one of them *executes*, which is the point: coverage said nothing about whether they decide anything. 926 tests (+3).
- **Verification:** `pnpm check` 0 (typecheck, build, 926 tests, 5/5 perf gates), `pnpm test:coverage` 0 on the rebased tree, `pnpm lint` 0, `pnpm typecheck` 0. Each mutant was applied to one line with the diff printed (`1 1` on `src/websocket.ts`, one hunk), and every file was restored from a `/tmp` copy with an explicit byte-identity assertion in the driver's own `finally`.
- **Risk / rollback:** three test cases, one driver-local helper, one comment block, one number in `AGENTS.md`. No `src/` behavior changes, so the three public-surface gates have nothing to see, and `git revert` removes the phase.
- **Next:** the same operand-level question where the ledger still has zero arms with a *multi-term* condition behind them — `cluster.ts`'s 14 and `data-bus.ts`'s 11 are all site-commented, so the productive form there is asking which comment's enumeration the file has outgrown, as Phase 169 did. `pnpm bench:browser` remains deferred on host load.
- **Update date:** 2026-09-24.


## Phase 173 / A guard whose every operand runs, and two of them decided nothing

- **Milestone / version:** test + shipped-comment + one repository rule after `0.21.21`. Branch `test/dedup-only-metrics-window` off `ee6c5b9`.
- **Where the target came from.** Phase 172's question — which operand of a multi-term guard is allowed to decide? — was turned into a scan: every `if (...)` in `src/` with two or more logical operators, ranked by operand count. Thirty-three. Eight of them have four terms — `data-bus.ts` holds four of those eight, and the other four are `environment.ts`'s storage-event frame validator, `replay-manager.ts`'s retention-sweep gate, `trace.ts`'s activity guard and one bounds validator in `validation.ts`. `trace.ts`'s `flushNow` activity check was taken first because it is the purest form: four counters OR'd to mean "was there activity".
- **Measured one operand at a time, whole suite, 928 tests.** `received > 0` dies to three cases, `dispatched > 0` to two, and **either** dedup term deleted leaves all 37 files green. Two single-counter cases were added — `emits a metrics window whose only activity is an accepted dedup` and `… is a suppressed dedup` — and each mutant now dies to its own.
- **Why it looked covered.** The only test that exercises those counters, `includes dedup outcomes in metrics windows`, records one acceptance and two suppressions **in the same window**. Delete either operand and the other still makes the disjunction true, so the test passes and the guard looks fully pinned. A joint test pins the sum; it never pins the halves. That is the same failure family as a coverage arm that executes but decides nothing — every operand of this guard is evaluated on every flush, so the report had no number to attach the gap to, which is why this leg outlived eleven releases of arm-hunting with the ledger otherwise closed.
- **Reach is a separate question from decidability, and the answer differs per leg.** `DedupManager.isDuplicate` has exactly one caller, `data-bus.ts`'s `handleTransportMessage`, and it runs one statement *before* `trace.recordReceived`. A suppression returns at that statement without recording a receive, so a window holding only suppressions is a state the bus produces (duplicate publications on an otherwise idle topic) and its unpinned operand was a live gap. An acceptance falls through to that `recordReceived` in the same synchronous block, and no timer can interleave between two statements of one task, so an acceptance-only window exists only where the reporter is called directly — the new test still pins the operand, and the comment at the guard says which half is which rather than letting "pinned by a test" imply "reachable from the API".
- **Repository rule, in `AGENTS.md`:** enumerate the single-operand deletions before calling a chain pinned, watch the joint test that raises both counters, and check reach separately from decidability because it is what distinguishes a live gap from a dormant one.
- **Probe queue the scan leaves open, in expected-yield order:** `environment.ts`'s storage-event frame validator (`!parsed || typeof parsed !== 'object' || typeof parsed.seq !== 'number' || !parsed.message` — a four-term guard on another same-origin script's input, so an operand that decides nothing here is a trust-boundary question, not just a coverage one), `replay-manager.ts`'s retention-sweep gate and `dedup-manager.ts`'s sweep gate (both `timer || !optionA || !optionB`, where the timer term may be dominated by the callers), and `validation.ts`'s three `typeof || isSafeInteger || <= 0` chains, where a test passing `0` and `'x'` never distinguishes the non-integer leg.
- **Ledger:** unchanged at **47** zero branch arms of **1958**, aggregate **99.02 / 97.59 / 99.27 / 99.69**, `trace.ts` still at its three (the sink arrow default and two compiler-required `?? 0` reads). **That non-movement is the finding**: two unpinned, one of them bus-reachable, behaviors existed in a module whose coverage had been read as closed, and no count moved when they were pinned. 928 tests (+2).
- **Verification:** `pnpm check` 0 (typecheck, build, 928 tests, 5/5 perf gates), `pnpm test:coverage` 0 on the rebased tree, `pnpm lint` 0, `git diff --check` clean. The four mutants were applied by a driver that locates each guard by full-condition match (asserting exactly one occurrence), prints the one-line diff, and restores every file byte-identically in its own `finally`; the driver had two bugs found on the way (a collision check that rejected a legitimate shortened-chain replacement, and re-reading the file between mutants on the same path so mutant N saw mutant N−1's text), both fixed before the reported numbers were taken.
- **Risk / rollback:** two test cases, one comment block at the guard, one `AGENTS.md` bullet. No behavior changes, so the three public-surface gates see nothing and `git revert` removes the phase.
- **Next:** the storage-event frame validator above it, then the release. Material for `0.21.22` is now Phases 171-173 (one guard refactor, six pinned legs, four corrected shipped claims) with no consumer-visible behavior change beyond comment text.
- **Update date:** 2026-09-24.


## Phase 174 / Four operands on a trust boundary, two of them unable to decide anything

- **Milestone / version:** test + shipped-comment + one repository rule after `0.21.21`. Branch `test/storage-event-envelope-operands` off `98cc30f`.
- **The target.** Phase 173's scan left a ranked queue and this was its first item: `createStorageEventChannel`'s envelope guard, four operands deep, reading a value that any same-origin script can put into `localStorage`. Probed the way the rule now says to — one operand deleted at a time, whole suite, before touching anything.
- **Before:** all four deletions left 928 tests green. Not one operand of a trust-boundary validator had ever been the thing that decided. The cause is the same shape Phase 173 had: the file's single malformed-envelope write is `{ nope: true }`, which fails both the `seq` test and the `message` test, so whichever of them survived still rejected the frame. A joint assertion pins the conjunction, never the halves.
- **After:** three writes exercise each field alone — an envelope with no `seq`, a `seq` that is the numeric string `"1"`, an envelope with no `message` — and the `seq` deletion and the `message` deletion each die to `ignores malformed payloads and foreign keys` (to different labelled assertions in it). The `seq` case also states a decision the code had only implied: a numeric string is rejected, not coerced.
- **The remaining two are not gaps, and the difference was measured rather than argued.** `typeof parsed !== 'object'` is never the first true operand for anything `JSON.parse` returns — every non-null primitive lacks a numeric `seq`, so the next test rejects it. `!parsed` *is* first for `null` (since `typeof null === 'object'`), but deleting it is unobservable too, because `null.seq` then throws inside the same `try` whose `catch` returns identically. A differential over 23 stored values (`null`, every JSON primitive, arrays including one wrapping a valid envelope, `{}`, an envelope with each field absent / null / boolean / a numeric string / `1e999`, and unparseable text) produced a byte-identical accept/drop vector for the guard as written and for either of the two deleted. The scratch probe that produced it was deleted after the run; the vector and its construction are recorded at the site.
- **Both stay, and the comment says what each is held against** — not an input, since none can reach them, but a future edit: dropping `!parsed` converts a contained rejection into an exception routed through `catch`, which only holds while the parse and the property reads share one `try`; dropping the object test starts accepting primitives the moment the `seq` test is relaxed. That is the AGENTS.md distinction between a dominated leg and a redundant one, applied for the first time on the receiver-trust side.
- **Checked and found standing, so it is not re-derived:** `docs/api.md` and `docs/zh/api.md` describe the *sender* side of this envelope (the per-channel nonce plus the monotonic sequence, and why same-value writes would otherwise be suppressed) and make no claim about the receiver's validation, so neither language needed a change; and the file's own test list confirms the other rejection legs are named — the foreign-key case, the no-echo-to-writer case, the legacy envelope without a `senderId`, and listener isolation.
- **Repository rule, in `AGENTS.md`:** name which of the three verdicts an operand has (pinned / cannot decide / live and unpinned), use a fixed-input differential to separate the middle one from the last, and when keeping a cannot-decide leg write the future edit that makes it load-bearing.
- **Ledger:** unchanged at **47** zero branch arms of **1958**, aggregate **99.02 / 97.59 / 99.27 / 99.69**, 928 tests. The whole guard is on a covered line with hot operands, so as in Phase 173 there was no count to move — which is the point the two phases keep making about the arm ledger.
- **Verification:** `pnpm typecheck` 0, `pnpm lint` 0, `pnpm test` 0 (37 files, 928 tests), `git diff --check` clean, all on the final tree; the four verdicts above were re-run *after* the site comment was written, on the committed state, because the comment shifts the guard's line number and the driver locates it by full-condition match. `pnpm check` 0 (typecheck, build, 928 tests, 5/5 perf gates) and `pnpm test:coverage` 0 ran on this same tree, after the verdicts above.
- **Risk / rollback:** three assertions in one existing test, one comment block, one `AGENTS.md` bullet. No behavior changes — the two deletions that could have changed acceptance were measured not to, and nothing else moved — so the public-surface gates see nothing and `git revert` removes the phase.
- **Next:** the same probe down the queue — `replay-manager.ts`'s retention-sweep gate and `dedup-manager.ts`'s sweep gate (both `timer || !optionA || !optionB`, where the timer term is the suspected cannot-decide leg), then `validation.ts`'s three `typeof || isSafeInteger || <= 0` chains. Material for `0.21.22` is now Phases 171-174.
- **Update date:** 2026-09-24.


## Phase 175 / Two managers, one guard shape, and only one file that learned to test the options separately

- **Milestone / version:** test work after `0.21.21`. Branch `test/dedup-sweep-option-legs` off `ebcbe3a`.
- **The target.** Next down Phase 174's queue: `DedupManager.start()`'s `this.sweepTimer || !this.enabled || !this.sweepMs`, and its sibling in `ReplayManager.start()`, which has the same shape with one more term. Probed the same way — each operand deleted alone, whole suite.
- **Result.** The dedup guard's first operand (the already-armed check) dies to `prunes quiet entries on the sweep interval and stops with the manager`; deleting either **option** leg left all 37 test files green. So the method's own doc — "No-op when disabled or no sweepMs was configured" — stated two behaviors nothing verified, the Phase 171 shape again: a sentence about a contract with no test on the other side of it. `arms no sweep timer when the manager is disabled, and none without a sweep interval` now feeds one configuration per leg, and each of the two deletions dies to it.
- **Why the second leg matters more than a missing prune:** an unset interval is not "no sweep", it is `setInterval(fn, undefined)`, and the delay in that call is the host's choice rather than a configured one. Recorded as the asymmetry between the two legs, without a number attached to it — no measurement in this repository fixes what a given browser does with an absent timeout, and a comment that claims one would be the kind of unverified absolute this project keeps having to retract.
- **The clean bill, which is the more useful half.** `ReplayManager.start()`'s four-term gate has **every** operand pinned: dropping `retentionTimer` dies to `sweeps durable history on the configured interval and stops on stop()`, and each of the three option legs dies to `start() is a no-op without a retention window, sweep interval, or clearBefore support` — one test, three configurations, one missing option each. That test is exactly the shape the dedup file lacked, and its absence there is the whole gap: the two managers are the same construct (`timer || option || option`), so parity between them was the cheapest place to look and the only place it was missing.
- **Ledger:** unchanged at **47** zero branch arms of **1958**, aggregate **99.02 / 97.59 / 99.27 / 99.69**. As in the three phases before it, the operands all evaluate on every call, so there was no zero count to move and no coverage signal that could have pointed at either gap. 929 tests (+1).
- **Verification:** `pnpm check` 0 (typecheck, build, 929 tests, 5/5 perf gates), `pnpm test:coverage` 0, `pnpm lint` 0, `pnpm typecheck` 0, `git diff --check` clean — all on this tree. The two verdict rows were re-run after the wording above was final, and each names its own killing test in the driver's output rather than being read off an exit code.
- **Risk / rollback:** one test. No behavior changes, so the public-surface gates see nothing and `git revert` removes the phase.
- **Next:** `validation.ts`'s three `typeof value !== 'number' || !Number.isSafeInteger(value) || value <= 0` chains, which are the last multi-term guards in the queue and the ones most likely to hide a joint-assertion gap of the same family (a test passing `0` and `'x'` never distinguishes the non-integer leg). Then `data-bus.ts`'s four-term guards. Material for `0.21.22` is now Phases 171-175.
- **Update date:** 2026-09-24.


## Phase 176 / Nine deletions, six real pins, and a pin that is thinner than the other five

- **Milestone / version:** shipped-comment + test-hygiene work after `0.21.21`. Branch `docs/validator-operand-verdicts` off `2786812`.
- **The target.** The last item in Phase 173's ranked queue, and the one that queue had flagged as the likeliest place to hide a joint-assertion gap: `assertPositiveSafeInteger`, `assertPositiveFiniteNumber` and `assertNonNegativeFiniteNumber` are three guards with one shape — `typeof` test, then a type-checking `Number.is*` predicate, then the sign. The suspicion was that a test feeding `0` and `'x'` never distinguishes the non-integer leg. Probed all nine single-operand deletions against the whole suite, per the rule.
- **Six of the nine die, and they die to the right shape.** Each is killed by an option-rejection case in `cluster.test.ts`, `data-bus.test.ts` or `replay-persistence.test.ts` — the predicate deletion and the sign deletion both die on their own, so no input here trips two operands the way Phase 174's single `{ nope: true }` write tripped two of four. These tests do feed several bad values inside one `it`, and that is fine: the joint-assertion trap is one *value* deciding two legs, not one *test* covering several values. No new test was needed for those six; the finding is that the option surface already had them.
- **The new datum is the unevenness.** Five of the six die to multiple named cases; `assertNonNegativeFiniteNumber`'s predicate leg dies to **exactly one** — `rejects a negative or non-finite loadWeighting weight`. Recorded at the site rather than smoothed over, because "six of nine pinned" reads uniform and is not. Checked that the one case is thin in count and not in kind: it feeds `NaN` and `Infinity`, which only the predicate rejects once the sign test is left behind, alongside `-1`, which only the sign rejects. Re-run on the final tree to confirm the tally after the wording was written.
- **Three survivors, and a differential says they are not gaps.** Deleting any of the three `typeof value !== 'number'` operands keeps 929 tests green for a reason that holds for every input: `Number.isSafeInteger` and `Number.isFinite` both answer false for a non-number without coercing, so any value that trips the `typeof` test trips the next operand too, with the same message. Proven, not argued — a 23-value vector (numeric strings, `''`, booleans, `null`, `undefined`, a prototype-less object, an array, a symbol, a `BigInt`, a function, a boxed `Number`, `NaN`, `±Infinity`, `0`, `-0`, `1.5`, a value past `MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`, `MAX_VALUE`) run across the three guards and the four variants (as written plus each `typeof` deleted) produced byte-identical accept/reject-and-message vectors. A scratch probe produced it and was deleted after the run; the vector and its result are at the site.
- **The operand stays, and the reason is now measured in both directions.** The substitution it defends against is writing the familiar global `isFinite(value)` where `Number.isFinite(value)` was — that coerces, and `eslint.config.js` configures no `no-restricted-globals` rule to catch it (verified: the string appears 0 times in the config, and no bare `isFinite(`/`isNaN(` call exists anywhere in `src/`, `tests/` or `scripts/`). Ran the counterfactual rather than asserting it: with the `typeof` operand in place the coercing swap kills **nothing**; with the operand also deleted, `rejects a non-positive or non-finite heartbeatIntervalMs` reddens because `heartbeatIntervalMs: '3000'` has become an accepted option. So this leg is held against an edit, not against an input.
- **Repository rule, appended to the existing `AGENTS.md` bullet:** that counterfactual is itself testable and worth running — make the swap the kept leg guards against and run it **both** with and without that leg, because "survives with it, dies without it" is the only evidence that a cannot-decide leg holds anything.
- **Ledger:** unchanged at **47** zero branch arms of **1958**, aggregate **99.02 / 97.59 / 99.27 / 99.69**, 929 tests. Every operand of all three guards evaluates on every call, so — the fourth phase in a row making this point — there was no count that could have pointed at either finding.
- **Verification:** `pnpm typecheck` 0, `pnpm lint` 0, `pnpm test` 0 (37 files, 929 tests), `pnpm test:coverage` 0, `git diff --check` clean, all on this tree. The nine verdict rows were re-run after the site comment was final, and the single thin-pin mutant was re-run once more after the unevenness sentence was added, each naming its killing test in the driver's output rather than being read off an exit code. The change is comment-only and that was proven twice: esbuild emits 130 lines for `main`'s file and 130 for this one, identical with comment lines stripped **and** identical raw — the latter because every block added here is a declaration header, which is the position Phase 171 measured esbuild to drop. So the raw match is the expected case, not extra evidence; the stripped comparison is the one that holds whatever the placement.
- **Risk / rollback:** three JSDoc/`//` blocks and one `AGENTS.md` sentence. Zero behavior change, and the gates that would notice one were run rather than assumed: `pnpm build` 0, `pnpm verify:compat` 0 ("preserves public exports and type metadata"), `pnpm verify:types` 0 ("6 entries, 90 importable names, surface closed"), `pnpm verify:pack` 0, and `pnpm test:perf` 5/5 — all on this tree. `git revert` removes the phase.
- **Queue state after this phase:** every multi-term guard named by Phase 173's scan has now been measured operand by operand except `data-bus.ts`'s four-term chains — `!this.started && !this.startPromise && !this.pendingStop && !this.transportReady`, `this.stopping || !this.started || this.suspended || this.status !== WORKER_STATUS.ERROR`, `this.transportReady && this.status !== WORKER_STATUS.ERROR && !droppedAfterConnect && !this.stopping`, and `!ready && this.started && !this.stopping && this.activeConfig !== undefined`. Those four are next, and unlike everything before them their operands are *state* rather than input, so no fixed input vector can serve as a differential; the reachability question has to be answered per operand from the lifecycle machine, which is also what makes a surviving mutant there ambiguous. Two by-products worth their own small phases: the `no-restricted-globals` rule that would remove the cause the `typeof` leg is held against (a one-line config addition, with the zero-current-findings check recorded above), and `cluster.ts`'s 14 / `data-bus.ts`'s 11 remaining zero arms.
- **Update date:** 2026-09-24.

Because squash-merge discards branch commit bodies, nothing incorrect reached `main`; the error is named here and in the PR body, which is where a correction survives.

Check it against the artifact before pushing (`git show <tag>:<generated doc>` pins a vintage; a directory listing pins a count); when it has already been pushed on an unmerged branch, correct it where it survives the squash; and re-derive a state phrase copied forward through log entries rather than copying it a fourth time.

## Phase 178 / Two state guards, an arming site two functions away, and a census instead of a vector

- **Milestone / version:** test + shipped-comment + one repository rule after `0.21.22`. Branch `test/data-bus-state-guard-operands` off `c502631`.
- **The target.** The first two of `data-bus.ts`'s four four-term chains — `stop()`'s "nothing to tear down" early return (`!started && !startPromise && !pendingStop && !transportReady`) and the recovery timer's callback gate (`stopping || !started || suspended || status !== ERROR`). They are the queue's last items and the only ones whose operands are *lifecycle state* rather than caller input, which is why six phases of input vectors do not carry over.
- **Sixteen mutants first, all four chains.** Every single-operand deletion run against the whole suite: **four die, twelve survive**. The four deaths are `stop()`'s `pendingStop`, the recovery timer's `status !== ERROR`, and two of the operation path's ready-shortcut (`transportReady`, whose deletion dies to eight named cases — the driver prints at most eight, so read that as a floor — and `droppedAfterConnect`, to two). This entry covers the first eight of the sixteen; the other eight are the next phase, deliberately, because that is where the survivors look live rather than dominated.
- **The replacement for a differential is a census.** Instrument each guard to record its operand fields at every evaluation, run the suite once, aggregate the distinct rows. `stop()` was called 7589 times across seven distinct vectors; the recovery callback ran 49 times across two. Compared against what each surviving operand needs to be the decider: **zero** observations of any of the six premises. That is the corroborating half, not the proof — so each verdict below is carried by an enumeration of assignment sites, and the site comment names both.
- **`stop()`'s `!started` turned out to be a third kind, which is the phase's most useful finding.** Its premise genuinely exists: every fresh `start()` holds `started=true` with `startPromise` still null, from the assignment until the install. But nothing between them runs caller code — `resetFailureState()` ends by *resolving* a promise, an epoch increment is arithmetic, and `openTransport()`'s synchronous prefix sets one field and returns a chain — so no `stop()` can ever be evaluated in that state. A dominated leg and an uninterruptible one read the same from the suite and need different comments: this one is held against an edit that puts a caller-visible seam back into that span, and the span is exactly what `updateStatus(CONNECTING)` is placed *after* the install to keep clear.
- **A rule stated at one of its two sites.** `reopenTransport()` already carries the sentence "Install the new lifecycle before publishing CONNECTING: a status handler can synchronously call stop()", and its own pairing of `startPromise`-then-`started` is deliberate. `stop()`'s operand had no such note, so the invariant existed in the code twice and in the prose once — the same one-copy-of-two failure the phrase-grep rule exists for, found by reading a guard instead of grepping a claim.
- **The recovery timer's three dead legs are killed by something outside the `if`.** All three (`stopping`, `!started`, `suspended`) survive their deletion because a recovery can only ever be armed from one `setTimeout` site, which sits inside `updateStatus()`'s `status === ERROR && this.started && !this.stopping` branch — so no timer can exist that was armed while either flag held — and neither flag can be raised afterwards without clearing the timer (`beginStop()` bumps the epoch and cancels in the same block, `suspendTransport()` cancels two lines after raising `suspended`, and the other `started = false` site resets it *before* the `updateStatus(ERROR)` that could arm, which its own comment already states). What each leg defends is therefore a *second arming site*, and the comments say so rather than calling them defensive.
- **The probe's own interference was a datum.** One test failed under the instrumented run — `settles stop() when the teardown failure cannot be reported either` — because that case replaces `console.warn` with a throwing shim and the census reported through `console.warn`. Nothing was wrong with the guard; the probe had walked into the hazard that `openTransport()`'s `before`-chain comment documents, and demonstrated it a second time from an unrelated edit. Recorded in the rule: a census that logs on a teardown path will break those tests, so read the failure before believing the count.
- **Ledger:** unchanged at **47** zero branch arms of **1958**, aggregate **99.02 / 97.59 / 99.27 / 99.69**, and **929 tests — this phase added none.** Like Phase 176, the output is eight classified operands, two of them re-cited with the test that already pins them, and no coverage number moved; reporting it as a coverage win would be false. The reason is the same as the four phases before it: every one of these operands is evaluated on every call.
- **Verification:** `pnpm typecheck` 0, `pnpm lint` 0, `pnpm test:coverage` 0 (37 files, 929 tests), `git diff --check` clean, all on the final tree. The eight A/B mutants were **re-run after both comments were written** and reproduced verdict for verdict (`pendingStop` and `status !== ERROR` killed by the same two named tests, six survivors), because the comments shift the guard's line number and the driver locates it by full-condition match. The change is comment-only and proven: `git diff --numstat` is `79 0` on `src/core/data-bus.ts`, and esbuild's output for the file is byte-identical to `main`'s both raw and with comment lines stripped (every added block sits in a statement slot, the position Phase 171 measured esbuild to drop).
- **Repository rule, in `AGENTS.md`:** for a state guard, run a flag-vector census instead of an input differential, pair the observed rows with the assignment enumeration, and name the future edit each kept leg is held against; two corollaries — a leg can be dominated by a statement two functions away rather than by a neighbouring operand, and a census that reports through `console.warn` will break the teardown tests that shim it.
- **Risk / rollback:** two comment blocks, one `AGENTS.md` bullet, no test and no behavior change; `git revert` removes the phase and the three public-surface gates have comment text to report and nothing else.
- **Next:** the remaining eight operands of the same probe — the operation path's ready-shortcut (`transportReady && status !== ERROR && !droppedAfterConnect && !this.stopping`, where deleting `transportReady` dies to eight cases and deleting `droppedAfterConnect` to two, but the `status` and `stopping` legs survive) and the demand-reopen chain (`!ready && started && !stopping && activeConfig !== undefined`, where all four survive). Those are the likely live gaps: an operand that decides whether a publication is written to a dead socket or queued behind a reopen has a consequence, so run the census there too and expect to write tests rather than only verdicts. Then the `no-restricted-globals` rule that removes the cause `validation.ts`'s kept `typeof` leg is held against. Material for `0.21.23` starts with this phase.
- **Update date:** 2026-09-24.


## Phase 179 / A stack trace turned a surviving mutant into a test, and three legs were already closed by the function they call

- **Milestone / version:** test + shipped-comment after `0.21.22`. Branch `test/transport-path-guard-operands` off `a7c0384`.
- **The target, and with it the end of the queue.** The last two of `data-bus.ts`'s four four-term chains: `runTransport()`'s fast path (`transportReady && status !== ERROR && !droppedAfterConnect && !stopping`) and the demand reopen under it (`!ready && started && !stopping && activeConfig !== undefined`). Phase 178 measured the first eight operands; this is the other eight, so the sixteen-mutant sweep the Phase 173 scan asked for is now complete, operand by operand, across the whole file.
- **What the sweep found, stated as a rate: one live gap in sixteen.** Across both phases, four operands were already pinned by a named test (`stop()`'s `pendingStop`, the recovery timer's `status`, and the fast path's `transportReady` and `droppedAfterConnect`), eleven are closed by construction, and exactly one — the fast path's `!this.stopping` — was live, unnamed, and fixable. That ratio is the honest argument for retiring this queue rather than extending it, and it is recorded so the next reader does not re-derive it.
- **The new pin.** Deleting `!this.stopping` handed the suite back green until `sends no unsubscribe to a transport while the bus is stopping` was written, and that test dies to exactly its own mutant. How it was found is the transferable part: the census recorded which flag vectors reach the guard, and printing a short stack on first sight of a premise row said *which production path* reaches it — `unsubscribeTransport()` ← a control frame ← `WorkerClusterRuntime.stop()`'s handoff, with `stopping` already raised by `beginStop()`. Nothing in the guard's own text hints at an unsubscribe-in-particular; the stack did.
- **The construction needed a second tab, and both earlier versions of the test passed anyway.** With one bus the handoff finds no remaining subscriber and *removes the route* instead of posting a control frame, so `runTransport` is never evaluated with `stopping` set and the assertion holds vacuously — green against the unmodified tree and green against the mutant. A second attempt, written to pin the `status !== ERROR` leg, failed the same way for a different reason: it parked its operation behind the recovery gate, which pre-empts the guard a few lines earlier. Both were caught by mutation-checking the test against its own mutant before committing either, which is the only check that distinguishes them.
- **Three of the demand-reopen chain's four legs are closed by the function it calls.** `reopenTransport()` opens with `stopping || activeConfig === undefined` and then reuses an in-flight `startPromise`, so deleting `!ready`, `!this.stopping` or `this.activeConfig !== undefined` assigns `ready` the very promise the fall-through would have produced. The census corroborates the first two directly — both premises occur in the existing suite (an opening already in flight, and a stopping bus) — and the callee's own comment already lists `runTransport()`'s demand reopen among the callers that re-check its guards, so the redundancy was documented from the far side and never brought back to this one. The premise that argument needs is stated at the site rather than assumed: the callee's reuse check excludes `startPromise === pendingStop`, the pairing the resume path creates deliberately.
- **`status !== ERROR` stays unpinned, and which half is established is named.** The premise (ready *and* errored *and* no gate *and* not stopping) is never evaluated by any of the 930 tests, and three routes were built to reach it through the public API — an error inside the cooldown after an explicit `start()`, the exhausted budget after a failed automatic attempt, and the same after a demand reopen. Each re-armed, because `start()`'s manual path runs `resetFailureState()` and a successful reopen clears the attempt counter. So the comment says "no route found, held against the gate branch above being relaxed or reordered", not "unreachable" — and the failure it prevents is the recurring quiet one: a publication handed to a socket that already reported `error`.
- **`this.started` on the reopen chain is the same verdict with a different reason:** `publish`/`subscribe` both pass `ensureStarted()`, which either restarts the bus (setting the flag first) or throws, and the internal callers' only status-driven fan-out is the reconnect arm. Held against a caller that reaches an operation without that gate.
- **Ledger:** **47** zero branch arms of **1958** before and after, aggregate **99.02 / 97.59 / 99.27 / 99.69**, 930 tests (+1). The pinned leg was on a line with hot operands, so — the sixth phase running — no count moved.
- **Verification:** `pnpm typecheck` 0, `pnpm lint` 0, `pnpm test:coverage` 0 (37 files, 930 tests), `git diff --check` clean, all on the final tree. The eight C/D mutants were **re-run after both comments were written** and reproduced: `transportReady` dies to eight cases, `droppedAfterConnect` to two, `!stopping` to exactly the new test, and five operands survive. `src/` is comment-only (`56 0`, esbuild output byte-identical raw and stripped at 926 emitted lines); the real change is the 46 added lines in `tests/data-bus.test.ts`.
- **Risk / rollback:** one test plus two comment blocks. The test adds a second runtime to `data-bus.test.ts` sharing one storage and channel hub; nothing else in the file touches those objects, and `git revert` removes the phase.
- **Next:** the per-operand guard queue is closed for `data-bus.ts`. What remains from Phase 173's scan is the zero-arm ledger with a multi-term condition behind it — `cluster.ts`'s 14 and `data-bus.ts`'s 11 — which is a different instrument (tier each arm, then reach it), plus the small standalone item this phase keeps adjacent to: a `no-restricted-globals` rule for `isFinite`/`isNaN`, which would remove the cause `validation.ts`'s kept `typeof` leg is held against and has zero current findings. Material for `0.21.23` is now Phases 178-179.
- **Update date:** 2026-09-24.


## Phase 180 / A justification that was a comment became a gate, and the comment had to be rewritten to say so

- **Milestone / version:** quality-gate + shipped-comment after `0.21.22`. Branch `chore/restricted-globals` off `5670153`.
- **The target.** The standalone item Phase 176 left behind. `validation.ts`'s three `typeof value !== 'number'` operands cannot decide anything — `Number.isSafeInteger`/`Number.isFinite` reject a non-number without coercing — and the only reason recorded for keeping one was that it catches a specific easy edit: writing the coercing global `isFinite(value)` where `Number.isFinite(value)` was, which nothing refused at the time because `eslint.config.js` configured no `no-restricted-globals` rule. That ordering is backwards. A leg whose entire justification is "someone might make this edit" should end up with a gate refusing the edit, not with a paragraph explaining why the edit would be bad.
- **The rule.** `no-restricted-globals` for `isFinite` and `isNaN`, in the `**/*.ts` block alongside `no-console`. It costs nothing today, which was checked before adding rather than after: the string appeared zero times in the config, and no bare `isFinite(`/`isNaN(` call exists anywhere in `src/`, `tests/` or `scripts/`.
- **A gate that cannot fail is not a gate, so the control was run.** `Number.isFinite(value)` was rewritten to `isFinite(value)` in `assertPositiveFiniteNumber` and `pnpm lint` reported exactly one error, at the call (`68:37 Unexpected use of 'isFinite'`), naming the coercion in the message; the file was then restored with `git checkout --` and the predicate's five occurrences confirmed back. Both readings are on the record because the useful half is the pair: clean tree zero findings, swap one finding.
- **Then the claim itself had to be hunted.** Two live copies said the rule does not exist — `src/utils/validation.ts`'s paragraph and the `AGENTS.md` bullet that cites this very measurement — and both are now false as written, so both were rewritten rather than deleted: the operand is defended twice, and the comment states which removal each defence covers (deleting the operand alone changes nothing today; deleting the rule re-opens the swap without touching the source). Five further mentions sit in `docs/progress.md` as the historical record of the phases that made the claim; those were left as they were written, with this entry as the pointer, since rewriting a log entry's description of what it observed would destroy the datum.
- **Why the leg is not deleted now that the rule exists.** Because the measured counterfactual still holds independently: with the `typeof` operand gone *and* the predicate intact, nothing changes; with the operand gone and the predicate swapped, `heartbeatIntervalMs: '3000'` is accepted. The rule protects this repository's source; the operand is what keeps the same mistake from being a silent behavior change in the shipped validator if the rule is ever loosened, and the measurement that says so is at the site.
- **Ledger:** unchanged at **47** zero branch arms of **1958**, aggregate **99.02 / 97.59 / 99.27 / 99.69**, 930 tests. No test was added and no source behavior moved; `src/utils/validation.ts` is comment-only, proven both ways (130 emitted lines identical raw and stripped, every added block in a position esbuild drops).
- **Verification:** `pnpm typecheck` 0, `pnpm lint` 0 on the clean tree and 1 error with the control applied, `pnpm test:coverage` 0 (37 files, 930 tests), `git diff --check` clean. Diff shape: `3 0` on `eslint.config.js` (the rule), `15 8` on `src/utils/validation.ts` (comment), `1 1` on `AGENTS.md`.
- **Risk / rollback:** one lint rule is a new refusal for future code, not a change to existing behavior — the public-surface gates, the frames, the storage keys and the defaults are untouched, so `git revert` removes the phase whole. The rule's own blast radius was measured first (zero current findings across `src/`, `tests/`, `scripts/`).
- **Next:** the per-operand guard queue and its by-products are both closed. What remains from Phase 173's scan is the zero-arm ledger with a multi-term condition behind it — `cluster.ts`'s 14 and `data-bus.ts`'s 11 — which needs the arm ledger's own instrument (tier each arm, then reach it) rather than the deletion probe. Material for `0.21.23` is now Phases 178-180.
- **Update date:** 2026-09-24.

One claim from this cycle's reading still has to be *measured* before it is written at a site: `pause()`'s `if (this.lifecycleListening)` false arm and `removeLifecycleListeners()`'s `if (!this.lifecycleListening) return` early return are **both** zero-count, and the reasoning that closes them as a pair is that `lifecycleListening` goes false in exactly one place (`stop()`), whose own `if (!this.started && !this.suspended) return` then blocks the second call from ever reaching either — i.e. `removeLifecycleListeners()` runs once per `stop()` and `pause()` is only reachable while the flag is true. That is a claim about two guards protecting each other, so it gets a mutation or a census, not a sentence.

## Phase 182 / cluster.ts's zero-arm ledger turned into two lifecycle fixes

- **Milestone / version:** `0.21.24` prepared on `test/cluster-zero-arm-ledger` (off `31ffc8e`), three commits: two `fix(cluster)` and one `docs(cluster)`.
- **What the ledger was for.** Phase 181's next item was to tier `cluster.ts`'s 14 zero-count branch arms the same way `data-bus.ts`'s had been tiered — verdict at each site, mutation or census behind each one. Fourteen arms were located and re-derived from `coverage/coverage-final.json` rather than from a previous phase's line numbers, and every one of them now has a written verdict.
- **What it found instead.** Two of those arms were the *visible edge of live defects*. `activate()` writes `started = true` and only then calls consumer code — the adapter's `createChannel`, and `handlers.onControl` for the storage-less self-SUBSCRIBE — before arming its heartbeat, so a `stop()`/pagehide arriving there had already run `pause()` and the remaining lines rebuilt what it removed. Measured on the unmodified tree: `coordinated: true` on a stopped runtime, its worker record back in flushed storage and seen by a peer at the first leaked tick (so no tab would ever TTL-prune it), and a `CONTROL/SUBSCRIBE` frame addressed to it after the stop landing in `assignedTopics`. Separately, a `stop()` issued inside `handlers.onResume` was dropped outright — `handlePageShow()` clears `suspended` on the statement before that callback, and `started` is set only by the `activate()` its generation bump skips — and the next hide/show pair re-fired `onResume` and restored `coordinated`.
- **Fixes.** `activate()` re-tests `started` after each of its two extension points and, in the first, closes the channel it built after the teardown instead of attaching it. `stop()`'s entry guard gains `!this.lifecycleListening`, which is the flag that actually means "something is still attached".
- **How the rest were settled.** A flag-vector census over one full suite run: four distinct `pause()` vectors, one each for `activate()`'s entry and `removeLifecycleListeners()`, two each for `reconcile()` and `writeRoute()` — with every probed flag reading false in at least one row, which is the control that makes the *absent* premise rows evidence. `reconcile()`'s `!started` was then re-probed with a stack print to check whether the fix had accidentally made it live: **0 occurrences**, so the verdict written at the site stands. Seven `tsc --noEmit` measurements for the legs whose deadness is a type question (1 / 1 / 1 / 1 / 1 / 1 / 5 errors), and the handoff owner guard's previously-claimed five re-measured on this tree rather than inherited.
- **Two tests were kept, three mutants checked.** Deleting the first activation check fails "a stopped runtime must not be registered"; deleting only the `this.channel = null` from its rollback fails `coordinated: false`; deleting the second check fails "no heartbeat may outlive the abandoned activation"; deleting the new `stop()` term fails its own test, while deleting either of `stop()`'s two original terms leaves all 933 green (both are implied by the new one, and kept on the asymmetry that a missing disjunct drops a teardown silently). The `channel?.close()` is recorded as the one half no assertion reaches, because a leaked port with no listener is invisible through the fake hub.
- **One shipped comment corrected.** The handoff's `if (!owner) continue` paragraph named "this method's own election" as one of three `?? this.currentRecord` fallbacks; that election has no such fallback, and the three are `subscribe()`'s plus two in `reconcileSubscriptions()` — verified by grepping the sites, not by re-reading the sentence.
- **Verification:** `pnpm check` 0 (typecheck, build, 933 tests, 5/5 perf gates), `pnpm lint` 0, `pnpm test:coverage` 0 (46 zero arms of 1963; 99.02 / 97.65 / 99.27 / 99.69), `verify:compat` / `verify:types` / `verify:pack` all 0 against `v0.21.23`, `pnpm bench` 0 (28/28), `tests/documentation.test.ts` 18/18 after the en/zh roadmap and api additions.
- **`pnpm bench:browser` deferred, with numbers.** The verify chain ran at load averages 34.33 / 50.13 / 62.83, so no sample was taken and `docs/benchmarks.md` stays at its last archived vintage rather than gaining a loaded row that would become the next release's baseline. This is the thirteenth consecutive cycle in that state; the standing decision at `docs/release-checklist.md` is to record the deferral with its load numbers.
- **Risk / rollback:** the behavior change is only observable to a consumer that stops a `WorkerClusterRuntime` from inside one of its own callbacks or from its adapter's `createChannel`. Rollback is reverting the two fix commits; no frame, storage key, export or default moved.
- **Next:** `cluster.ts` is closed — 13 zero arms left, each with a verdict naming what decides it. The same tiering has not been written at each site for the remaining 33, which the fresh per-file dump distributes as `data-bus.ts` 11 (already verdicted in Phases 173-179), `replay-persistence.ts` 6, `replay-manager.ts` 5, `trace.ts` 3, `workers/port-reaper.ts` 3 (legs behind the `Number.isFinite` payload validation the 0.21.9 fix touched), `websocket.ts` 2, and one each in `centrifuge-session.ts`, `centrifuge.ts` and `core/version.ts` — the last of those already carries its own verdict (no tool in this repository consumes `src/` without passing the bundle-time define, so the `''` arm is a shape the harness cannot reach rather than a case nobody exercised), which is the target state for the other 32.

## Phase 184 / a fan-out that did not terminate: subscriber mutation during dispatch

- **Milestone / version:** `0.21.25` prepared on `fix/dispatch-snapshot` (off `65a7eca`), one `fix(data-bus)` commit plus this release bookkeeping.
- **Where it came from.** Phase 183 closed with a negative result: `data-bus.ts`'s lifecycle methods already re-test their own liveness on the far side of every consumer call, because the bus has a `lifecycleEpoch` and `WorkerClusterRuntime` had nothing equivalent. The one thing that probe did surface was unasserted behavior one layer down — a `bus.stop()` from inside a subscriber handler let the current message finish fanning out. Following that thread into `dispatch()` found the real defect, which was not about `stop()` at all.
- **The defect.** `dispatch()` iterated the live per-topic `Set` (and the live `topicHandlers` Map for wildcard patterns). `Set` iteration visits entries appended after the cursor and skips entries deleted before it, so a handler that registered *another* handler for its own topic was served the message that caused the registration. That is not merely surprising, it does not terminate: measured on the unmodified tree, one publication invoked **500** handlers (the probe's ceiling, not a bound the library imposes) and the next one delivered to **999**, because the registrations persist across messages. The mirror case also held: an `unsubscribe()` from an earlier handler removed a later one from a delivery already in flight (the pair delivered `['first']`).
- **Why no earlier pass found it.** The first probe used a named function, and re-subscribing the same reference is a no-op by `Set` identity — it measured `invocations: 1` and read as "not a problem". Rewriting it to register a distinct closure per invocation produced the 500/999 numbers. The lesson is about probes, not about this file: a probe that returns the safe answer on its first shape has tested that shape, not the question.
- **Fix.** Both passes are collected before the first handler runs, so a publication is delivered to the subscribers that existed when its delivery began, and a late `unsubscribe()` takes effect on the next publication instead of mid-message.
- **Verification.** `pnpm test` 936 passed (933 before, unchanged by the fix); `pnpm typecheck` 0; `pnpm test:perf` 5/5; `pnpm test:coverage` 0 with **46** zero-count arms of **1963** and aggregate 99.02 / 97.65 / 99.27 / 99.69 — no movement, because both arms of every branch added here were already exercised. Each new test's failure message is the measurement: `expected 500 to be 1`, `expected [ 'first' ] to deeply equal [ 'first', 'second' ]`, `expected [ 'exact', 'pattern' ] to deeply equal [ 'exact' ]` — all three confirmed against the reverted `dispatch()` before the fix was kept, and the runaway case is written with an explicit ceiling so a regression reports a count rather than hanging the runner.
- **Hot path sized directly.** None of the five `tests/perf-gate.test.ts` gates covers dispatch, so the snapshot was measured with a best-of-seven / 200k-iteration script: **9-23 ns per dispatch** for 1-20 handlers and **+15 ns** for a matching wildcard pattern with two handlers, against shipped per-message figures in the tens of microseconds.
- **Docs.** One bullet added to `docs/api.md` and the same one to `docs/zh/api.md` (list-item parity is gated by `tests/documentation.test.ts`), stating the delivery-set contract in the `subscribe()` list.
- **Risk / rollback:** revert `b17531b`. The observable delta is confined to registering or releasing a handler from inside a handler for the same topic — the shape that grew without bound.
- **`pnpm bench:browser`:** to be taken or deferred at the pre-tag gate with its load numbers recorded; the host has been loaded for the last fourteen cycles.
- **Next:** the 21 zero-count arms in the files Phase 182's method has not reached yet (`replay-persistence.ts` 6, `replay-manager.ts` 5, `trace.ts` 3, `workers/port-reaper.ts` 3, `websocket.ts` 2, `centrifuge-session.ts` 1, `centrifuge.ts` 1). And the probe lesson above is worth a rule: when a probe's first shape measures safe, re-write it with distinct identities before believing it.
- **Update date:** 2026-09-25

## Phase 186 / the scan that scheduled the work was the defect of the pass

- **Milestone / version:** `0.21.26` prepared on `fix/retry-generation-writer` (off `367999a`), one `fix(replay)` comment commit plus this release bookkeeping.
- **What it was supposed to be.** Phase 185's Next item named 14 zero-count arms "still lacking a verdict at their site". That list was wrong, and wrong in a way worth writing down: the scan that produced it decided *no verdict* by reading the single line above each arm, while every verdict in this repository is a five-to-fifteen-line comment that states the measurement closing the arm. Re-derived against fresh coverage, the ledger is **46 zero-count arms of 1963**, and **all 46 already carry a verdict at the site** — `cluster.ts` 13, `data-bus.ts` 11, `replay-persistence.ts` 6 (its four `settled` latches plus `open()`'s two `dbPromise` guards), `replay-manager.ts` 5, `trace.ts` 3, `workers/port-reaper.ts` 3, `websocket.ts` 2, `centrifuge-session.ts` 1, `centrifuge.ts` 1, `core/version.ts` 1. Reading the reported sites with a window turned a re-audit of closed ground into one real find.
- **The find.** Four comments in `replay-manager.ts` described the persistence-retry cancellation generation as bumped "on suspend/stop". The class defines *both* of those methods, and `stop()` never touches the field — it clears the retention-sweep timer and nothing else; `suspend()` is the field's only writer. Checked against `0cb8572`, the commit that split this file out, `stop()` already had its current body and `suspend()` was already the sole writer, so this is not a sentence that drifted from a later change; it was false the day it was written. What *is* true lives one level up: `CrossTabDataBus` has no `suspend()` method, and it reaches `replayManager.suspend()` from two sites — the cluster's `onSuspend` handler (`data-bus.ts:386`) and `beginStop()` (`:1366`) — so a hidden tab and a stopped bus both do cancel, which is precisely why no test ever contradicted the pair: the covering test is `tests/data-bus.test.ts:5346`, "cancels a pending persistence retry when the bus stops".
- **What the correction says now.** The field names its one writer; `suspend()`'s docstring names the two bus call sites that reach it and keeps the original "hidden tab or stopped bus" motivation; `stop()`'s says it cancels nothing and records that its only caller in `src/` is `suspend()` (the class is internal — `ReplayManager` appears nowhere in `src/index.ts`, so no consumer can hold the wrong model); `withPersistenceRetry()`'s and the inline comment drop the pair for `suspend()`.
- **Fourteen other enumeration claims audited in the same pass, and the ones that held.** These are the sentences a later reader acts on, so the correct ones are recorded too: `assignedTopics` "grown by exactly three writers" (`.set` at 1096/1200/1468 ✓); `confirmRoute()` "exactly three call sites" (1097/1201/1469 ✓); `transportReady = false` "exactly five places" (734/845/1413/1769/1898 ✓); `pendingStop` "written in exactly four places" (778/843/1415/1798) with its twin at `:1383` "assigned non-null in exactly two" (843/1798 ✓ — the pair is consistent because two of the four write `null`); `suspended = true` one place (1767 ✓); `stopPromise` non-null one place (1319 ✓); `autoStart` one participating site (400 ✓); `metricsActive` "seven readers" (284/305/328/343/381/385/412 ✓) with `stopped` read in two (274/407 ✓); `connectPromise` "assigned in exactly two statements" (264 in `start()`, 338 in `stop()` ✓); `startHeartbeat()`'s "only caller" (250 ✓) with `backend` nulled only via `resetBackend()`, whose two callers both `clearHeartbeat()` first (198, 354 ✓); `scheduleRetry()`'s "only caller" (137, inside `flush()`, which cancels on entry at 100 and breaks at 138 ✓); PortReaper's `schedule()` caller set (63/103/114 + `reap()`; `touch()` at 74 is gated and does not schedule ✓), its "`dispose()` has no Worker-side caller" (zero in `src/` ✓, and recorded at `docs/configuration.md:219` and `docs/zh/configuration.md:212` ✓), and `computeMinHeartbeat`'s "grep: zero hits" in `tests/` ✓; `topicHandlers` written only at 972, behind `assertPublicTopic` at 956 ✓; `pendingReplayPersistence` pushed only at 150 ✓; `queueStartAfterStop()`'s single caller at 416 ✓.
- **Docs.** `AGENTS.md` gained the rule this cycle actually teaches: a *scan* is a probe, so it needs the control a probe needs — run it on a site known to be answered and check it reports "present" before its output becomes a task list — plus the pair-shorthand half (when a comment names two methods as doing the same thing, check each name in the class that owns the thing, because a pair can be true of callers and false of callees while every test passes). `docs/roadmap.md` and `docs/zh/roadmap.md` gained mirrored `0.21.26 delivered scope` sections, and both lead lines now name `0.21.26`.
- **Verification:** `pnpm check` 0 (typecheck, build, **936** tests, 5/5 perf gates), `pnpm lint` 0, `pnpm test:coverage` 0 with the ledger unmoved at **46 of 1963** and aggregate 99.02 / 97.65 / 99.27 / 99.69 — byte-identical to `0.21.25`'s, as it must be for a diff with no code in it. `git diff -U0 src/` with every comment line filtered out returns nothing, which is the statement that this is a comment-only change. `tests/documentation.test.ts` 18/18.
- **The shipped-surface control, taken rather than assumed.** The corrected sentences were grepped in the built tree and appear in `dist/core/replay-manager.d.ts`, in the ESM chunk `dist/chunk-WKOCDMCH.js` and in both CJS bundles (`dist/cjs/index.cjs`, `dist/cjs/centrifuge.cjs`) — esbuild keeps comments in the JS, and every one of those paths is in `package.json` `files`. This is the artifact where the claim *would* have shown up, named so the reading is not "no evidence". → **PARTLY RETRACTED in Phase 188.** The grep matched this release's two *class-member* JSDocs; its inline comment inside `withPersistenceRetry()` is absent from the bundles and reaches consumers only through the published `.js.map` sources — as does every statement-slot comment in the tree, including ones that predate this finding, so it is esbuild's placement rule rather than a regression. `AGENTS.md` now carries the position rule and asks the question per artifact.
- **No test added, and that is a classification rather than a gap.** An assertion that `ReplayManager.stop()` cancels nothing would characterize an internal method with one caller instead of pinning a contract; the useful fact is the writer count, which is what the field's comment now states.
- **`pnpm bench:browser` deferred, with numbers: the seventeenth consecutive cycle.** Load averages 24.82 / 25.04 / 30.72 on 8 cores at this entry, so no sample was taken and `docs/benchmarks.md` was not regenerated.
- **Risk / rollback:** comment-only; revert this branch's single fix commit. Nothing consumer-visible moved — no export, frame, option, default or storage key changed, and `verify:compat` / `verify:types` / `verify:pack` run against `v0.21.25` below.
- **Next:** the remaining claims of this shape that a window-read has not yet adjudicated — the *behavioral* assertions inside the verdicts rather than their counts: `cluster.ts:464` ("the only way this arm was reached", which the Phase 182 fix could have changed), `:604`, `:1248`, `:1411` (the `knownTopics` absolute, which sits next to `assignedTopics`' own key→plaintext map), `:1715`; `data-bus.ts:973`, `:1828`, `:1906`, `:2012`; `trace.ts:28`, `replay-pruning.ts:17`, `environment.ts:44`, `port-reaper.ts:26/69/180`, `storage-batch.ts:42`. Also still open from the ledger's own terms: the arms whose consequence is a behavior no test names yet, which is the in-scope queue item `AGENTS.md` records.

## Phase 187 / 0.21.26 shipped: the release whose own scheduling step was the finding

## Phase 188 / three lifecycle comments re-checked, and one of them was right for the wrong reason

- **Milestone / version:** `0.21.27` prepared on `docs/cluster-window-provenance` (off `29b7dbd`), two `docs(...)` commits plus this release bookkeeping. Comment-only — `git diff -U0 src/` with every comment line filtered out returns nothing.
- **What this pass was for.** Phase 186 closed the ledger's *counts*; its Next line named the remaining work as the *behavioral* sentences inside those verdicts — the ones that say *why* a window is closed, not how many writers a field has. Three of them turned out to be different kinds of wrong, which is why this is a release rather than a note.
- **1. A reason that was false while the code was right.** `reconcile()`'s guard note explained its REGISTRY leg as closed because nothing between `pause()` clearing `started` and `pause()` removing the message listener "can hand the stack to consumer code". That span is three statements — a boolean assignment, `this.environment.clearInterval(this.heartbeatHandle)`, and a `heartbeatHandle` write — and the middle one is a call into **adapter** code, which this same file's `activate()` comment treats as consumer-supplied and untrustable (that premise is what the two abandonment checks are built on). So the window is not closed by an absence of calls; the `if (!this.started) return` guard closes it. The old phrasing had argued, by accident, that the guard it was defending was redundant.
- **2. A covered arm whose origin was an argument, now a measurement.** `pause()`'s null-`heartbeatHandle` branch is reached only from the activation window — claimed, and unfalsifiable from coverage because the arm is covered either way. Instrumenting the branch with a stack print and running the suite (`pnpm test`, exit 0) printed **exactly two lines and no third**: one origin inside a wrapped `createChannel`, one inside the storage-less self-SUBSCRIBE's `handlers.onControl` — one per activation seam, matching 'abandons activation when the channel adapter tears the runtime down mid-start' and 'abandons the heartbeat when a handler stops the runtime during the storage-less re-subscribe'. Both names are quoted at the site, so a third origin becomes a visible difference instead of a re-derivation. The probe lived in a scratch copy and was reverted with `git checkout --`; the shipped artifact is the comment.
- **3. A number that rotted without contradicting anything.** `reopenTransport()`'s note carried "0 of 5041 calls in the coverage run", written in `b0354e4` (confirmed with `git log -S`). The same lookup on this tree — `coverage/coverage-final.json`'s function count — reads **5046**. The figure only ever supported *hot method, cold arms*, a reading that survives any drift, which is exactly what makes a stale constant dangerous: it looks like evidence and calibrates the next reader against a run that no longer exists. The sentence now names the lookup; `AGENTS.md` gained the general rule beside the existing one about numeric adjectives.
- **A fourth finding, about this repository's own claim on where comments ship.** Grepping one built tree for the sentences above produced a clean split: a **class-member JSDoc** (`0.21.26`'s `stop()` note) appears in `dist/core/replay-manager.d.ts`, in the shared ESM chunk *and* in both CJS bundles, while every **statement-slot** comment — this cycle's three, `0.21.26`'s own inline comment inside `withPersistenceRetry()`, and the long-standing "Order matters: release local subscriptions…" note — reaches the published package only through the `.js.map` files' embedded sources (`files: ["dist"]` does publish those). The third case is the control that keeps this from reading as a regression. So Phase 187's shipped-surface bullet now carries a PARTLY RETRACTED marker, and `AGENTS.md`'s "how prose reaches consumers" rule gained its position half: ask per artifact, not per tree.
- **Claims that held, recorded so they are not re-hunted.** `reconcile()`'s "four callers" (426 activate, 430 heartbeat, 1002 visibility — gated at 1000 — and 1052 REGISTRY, ungated) ✓; `cluster.subscribe()`'s "the other caller is `start()`'s replay loop" — exactly two sites ✓; `trace.ts`'s "a no-arg reporter 300 times per run" ✓ derived rather than guessed (`tests/property.test.ts` builds one in a 200-round loop and one in a 100-round loop); `pendingStop`'s two apparently conflicting counts are consistent because two of its four writes assign `null` ✓. And one candidate that never existed: a figure carried in session notes about `cluster.ts` ("1249 of the method's 1252 entries") matches nothing in the repository — grep says the sentence was invented downstream, so "quote the phrase, do not trust the report" catches fabrications in the agent's own notes as well as a subagent's.
- **Verification:** `pnpm check` 0 (typecheck, build, **936** tests, 5/5 perf gates), `pnpm lint` 0, `pnpm test:coverage` 0 with the ledger at **46 zero-count arms of 1963** and aggregate **99.02 / 97.65 / 99.27 / 99.69** — identical to `0.21.26`'s, which is what a diff with no branches in it must produce. `pnpm build` 0, `tests/documentation.test.ts` 18/18, `pnpm bench` 0 (28/28), `verify:compat` ("`0.21.27` preserves public exports and type metadata from `v0.21.26`"), `verify:types` ("6 entries, 90 importable names, surface closed"), `verify:pack` ("verified ESM/CJS root and subpath consumers from `cross-tab-worker-databus-0.21.27.tgz`"), `RELEASE_TAG=v0.21.27 node scripts/verify-release-version.mjs` 0, `git diff --check` clean.
- **`pnpm bench:browser` deferred, with numbers: the eighteenth consecutive cycle.** Load averages **29.71 / 54.40 / 54.50** on 8 cores at this entry, so no sample was taken and `docs/benchmarks.md` was not regenerated.
- **Risk / rollback:** comment-only; reverting this branch's squash commit is the whole rollback. No consumer-visible surface moved, and the corrected statements are about internal methods, so no `docs/` page carried them.
- **Next:** the same treatment for the remaining behavioral sentences named by Phase 187 — `cluster.ts`'s "it is the only write in that window" (the `confirmRoute()`-before-the-handler and `notifyRegistry()`-through-`send()` halves are each checkable), `data-bus.ts`'s "the only handler this opening ever gets" and its `1001`-row claim, `storage-batch.ts`'s "test-only as a reader", `port-reaper.ts`'s three, `replay-pruning.ts`, `environment.ts`, `trace.ts`'s "the only category this mode excludes". Plus the instrument this cycle proved cheap and general: a stack-printing probe over one suite run answers "what can reach this line" for any synchronous extension point, which is the question several ledger verdicts answer without one.
- **Update date:** 2026-09-25
